title: Reservoir Computing Foundations
intro: Reservoir computing trains only a linear readout on the states of a fixed, driven dynamical system; everything quantum reservoir computing does is this recipe with a quantum system as the reservoir. This chapter makes the classical theory exact: echo state networks, the echo state property, memory and processing capacity, physical reservoirs and the benchmark tasks.

blocks.text: Quantum reservoir computing is an old idea in a new material. The old idea, reservoir computing, says that a fixed dynamical system, driven by an input stream and left untrained, can serve as the memory and the nonlinear mixing stage of a learning machine, provided you train a simple linear readout on what it does. The new material is a quantum system: a few qubits, a spin ensemble, a bath of photons. Before the quantum pages can say anything precise, the classical idea has to be understood properly, and that is this chapter's job.

The chapter assumes you have read Getting Started (#/qrc/start), which taught the machine learning from zero and ended with a quantum reservoir computed by hand. Here the same ideas are made exact. Each page answers one question that the quantum chapters keep asking: what is the standard model and what are its knobs? when does a driven system forget its start? how much can it remember and compute? which real devices have been used? and how do you score the result honestly?

The five pages build on each other, though the last two can be read in either order. Each page has the same shape: what you need first, what you will be able to do, full sections with worked examples, checks as you go, a worked problem that ties the page together, key points, problems with solutions, and sources. Allow about 90 minutes to two hours per page if you work the examples and run the code; about five to ten hours for the chapter.

items: Echo State Networks (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-networks): the canonical reservoir. The update rule built unit by unit and worked by hand, ridge regression seen three ways (normal equations, singular values, dual form), the five hyperparameters and what each does to memory and nonlinearity, a complete network on NARMA10 (NMSE 0.154 with 50 units, 0.081 with 200, against 0.346 for linear regression on the inputs it needs), and teacher forcing for generation.

The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property): why a reservoir must forget its starting state, the proof that a tanh network with $\sigma_{\max}<1$ does, why the spectral radius is the practical criterion although it is not a proof, how strong inputs rescue a network with $\rho>1$, how to measure forgetting with a Lyapunov exponent, and why a unitary quantum system can never forget.

Memory and Processing Capacity (#/qrc/foundations/memory-and-capacity): the memory function computed exactly for one unit, the proof that memory capacity cannot exceed the number of independent features, information processing capacity with Legendre polynomials, the memory-nonlinearity trade-off with measured tables, and how finite data and noise bias estimates.

Physical Reservoirs (#/qrc/foundations/physical-reservoirs): the checklist for a physical reservoir, a simulated ripple tank in which the sensor supplies the nonlinearity, virtual nodes built from a single delay-loop node by hand, and the engineering limits (bandwidth, noise, partial observation) that become harsher for quantum devices.

Benchmark Tasks and Evaluation (#/qrc/foundations/benchmark-tasks): the evaluation protocol, metrics and their traps, the standard tasks (memory, NARMA, parity, Mackey-Glass, channel equalisation), and the ladder of baselines a result must climb.

blocks.text: These are the relations the chapter builds up to. Each page derives its own; here they are in one place.

blocks.caption: The reservoir: state update with leak rate $a$, fixed random weights, input $u_k$.
The only learning: ridge regression on the recorded features $Z$, the targets $Y$.
Forgetting: two copies fed the same input converge if $\sigma_{\max}(W)<1$; the echo state property in its provable form.
Memory capacity: the sum over delays of how well the input $d$ steps ago can be read out, at most the number of independent features.
Information processing capacity: the same budget shared among memory and nonlinear functions of the past.
The score: 0 is perfect, 1 is no better than the average.

blocks.text: How this chapter connects to the quantum ones
Every classical idea here has a quantum counterpart, and the later chapters are largely about how the counterpart behaves differently.

items: The state $x_k\in\mathbb{R}^N$ becomes a density matrix $\rho_k$, and the update becomes a completely positive trace-preserving map $\rho_k = \mathcal{T}_{u_k}(\rho_{k-1})$ (Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels)). The features are expectation values $\operatorname{Tr}(O_i\rho_k)$.

The echo state property becomes contractivity of that map. A unitary alone never forgets, so a quantum reservoir needs a reset, a measurement or a bath (Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points), Dissipation as a Resource (#/qrc/models/dissipation-as-resource)).

The number of units $N$ becomes the number of independent observables you can read, in principle $4^n-1$ for $n$ qubits, but each costs measurement shots (Readout and Multiplexing (#/qrc/models/readout-and-multiplexing), Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action)).
The virtual nodes of a delay loop reappear as $V$ samples of the quantum system between inputs.
The benchmarks are the same, so classical baselines are directly comparable, and the baseline rules of Benchmark Tasks and Evaluation (#/qrc/foundations/benchmark-tasks) apply with full force.

The state of a quantum reservoir lives in a space that grows as $2^n$ for $n$ qubits. Whether this large space is an asset or a liability for learning is the subject of Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability).

blocks.text: If you already know echo state networks well, still read the echo state property and capacity pages: the quantum chapters use the contraction picture and the capacity bound constantly.

items: $u_k$ or $s_k$: the scalar input at step $k$ (the quantum pages use $s_k\in[0,1]$ because it sets a qubit amplitude).
$x_k\in\mathbb{R}^N$: the feature vector read at step $k$ (the reservoir state for an ESN, expectation values for a quantum reservoir).
$y_k$ is the target and $\hat y_k$ the readout's prediction; washout, training and test windows are consecutive blocks of one input stream.
MC is the linear memory capacity, $C_{\mathrm{tot}}$ the total information processing capacity, NMSE the mean squared error divided by the target variance.

blocks.text: The next chapter, Open Quantum Systems Toolkit (#/qrc/open-systems), builds the mathematics of density matrices, channels and measurement that turns the classical echo state property into its quantum form. Then Quantum Reservoir Models (#/qrc/models) puts the pieces together into working quantum reservoirs, starting with The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir).
